sentences.text: Tyson Fury will fight Anthony Joshua on 11 December in Cardiff Tyson Fury says he was diagnosed with schizophrenia soon after his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: British heavyweight Fury, 38, says he heard voices in his head threatening to hurt him and his family.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: In a documentary which will be released by Netflix on Friday, Fury and wife Paris describe how he was diagnosed after being admitted to hospital with a suspected heart attack in June 2016.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury says.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "It was like a living version of the pits of hell.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "The anxiety was crippling me.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder." Doctors said Fury had suffered an anxiety attack.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: Fury recalls hearing the radio talking to him, and begging Paris to get him out of the hospital because "the Illuminati" wanted him.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: In the period after his victory over Klitschko, Fury gained weight and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "It got that bad I was hearing voices in my mind," he says.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "I wouldn't be able to sit and have a conversation because I'd be hearing stuff in my mind.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "I didn't know where to turn and no-one knew what to do.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: I really needed help, or check into rehab or something.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "I never got a break from it for years.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: I wanted to be what I thought was normal again." After Fury was released from hospital, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder was confirmed.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: The NHS describes schizophrenia , external as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: It says the main symptom of bipolar disorder , external is extreme changes to your mood.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: Fury describes a "turning point" in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked," he says.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on.
sentences.article_title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

sentences.text: "I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, 'I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I'm a fat mess addicted to alcohol'." He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training.

sentences.text: Prof Fiona Gilbert, who is co-leading the trial, will assess if AI can improve breast cancer diagnosis Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Recruitment to the EDITH trial , external has already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Shirley Essex says routine breast screening saved her life Prof Fiona Gilbert, department of radiology, University of Cambridge, honorary consultant at Addenbrooke's Hospital, and co-chief investigator said: "Millions of women have a mammogram each year and only a small number, less than 1%, will have cancer.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Shirley Essex, 70, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer a year ago after a routine screening appointment.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: She had surgery and radiotherapy, but did not require chemotherapy.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: She told the BBC that her mammogram had saved her life: "I was astonished to be told I had cancer because I did not have any symptoms." Shirley is not part of the study but is passionate about the importance of screening.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: "I feel so lucky my cancer was detected early.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: It was my last routine mammogram, so if I had not attended, my cancer would have kept growing," she said.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Women will be informed about the study when they receive a routine screening invitation, but will not be obliged to take part.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: The trial will not change what happens during a breast screening appointment.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Instead, it will test whether AI-assisted tools could replace one of the two human specialists reviewing mammograms.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Researchers say machine-learning software can be trained on millions of previous images in order to detect patterns, and so potentially find subtle changes in breast tissue that might be missed by the human eye.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: In one arm of the trial, an AI programme will grade images before they are sent to NHS experts.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: In another, it will review images afterwards.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: The £11m trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: It is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working with NHS England.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: "Every scan will still be seen by a specialist, and if proven effective, it could ensure women get the diagnosis and treatment they need sooner," he said.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Four AI companies are involved in the trial, which is expected to last around three years.
sentences.article_title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial

sentences.text: Cape Schanck, Victoria, dates from 1862 and depicts the dramatic coastline at the southernmost tip of Australia's Mornington Peninsula A rediscovered 19th Century oil painting bought for £20 in a charity shop could be auctioned for up to £20,000.

sentences.text: Cape Schanck, Victoria, by Russian-Swiss artist Nicholas Chevalier, was discovered in a charity shop in Maidenhead, Berkshire.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: It was brought to the attention of Adrian Biddell at London's Olympia Auctions, who established the painting was a Chevalier work that had been missing for 160 years.

sentences.text: "To find it now, quite unexpectedly, in a corner of the British high street, is an extraordinary find," he said.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: The painting dates from 1862 and depicts the dramatic, rugged coastline at the southernmost tip of Australia's Mornington Peninsula, about 60 miles (96.5km) south of Melbourne.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: The auction house said only two of five en plein air - meaning painted directly in front of the landscape it depicts - views of Cape Schanck by Chevalier that year were known to have survived until now.

sentences.text: Both are in the collection of the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: It said the charity shop buyer had liked the landscape but had not been familiar with the artist or the painting's value.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: Its appearance "resolves a longstanding gap in the documented history of Chevalier's work", it said.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: It was leading Chevalier expert Simon Gregg who confirmed its whereabouts had previously been recorded as "unknown" in his catalogue of the artist's work.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: "This was definitely painted en plein air," he said.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: "This was Chevalier's typical modus operandi." Gregg added: "Most of the oil sketches have not survived, hence my delight that this one has shown up." Biddell said Chevalier "was a remarkable visual talent, with an extraordinary ability to capture the drama, power and sheer scale of the natural world".
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: "The discovery of Cape Schanck, Victoria is hugely exciting," he said.
sentences.article_title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in charity shop

sentences.text: Ffion, Yugraj and Jessica say being ghosted has become a common part of applying for jobs Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training -  those dubbed as Neets - this week.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive?
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not." Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: "With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: The Milburn report , external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from".
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: "It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: "It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Ellie says constructive feedback is always preferable to being ghosted "If you are applying for hundreds of jobs and never getting anything, I think something is going wrong...
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: You can't fix something unless you know what the problem is." There are things applicants can do to improve their chances and avoid ghosting, such as tailoring their CV to each job and not submitting "hundreds and hundreds of applications" that all look the same, Burton adds.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Candidates should also never take being ghosted personally, she adds.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: "Not hearing back doesn't mean you aren't a great candidate.
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Put it down to experience and move on."
sentences.article_title: Hundreds of applications, no replies: Inside the job ghosting problem‌

sentences.text: Photonic chips use light instead of electrons to process data "Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago." American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe , external , with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology." ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "Europe has a strong position in photonics research.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity , external , which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy".
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: In June this year, US photonics company Coherent announced what it called "the world's first and largest volume-production six-inch indium phosphide manufacturing platform" at its plant in Sherman, in Texas.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: The expansion is backed by chip manufacturing giant Nvidia , external , as well as $50 million public funds under the US Chips Act.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: It's an illustration of how quickly the market is moving, and how central photonic chips could be to the continuing race to retain an influential stake in AI and technological development more generally.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Europe's bid to establish itself as a global leader in photonic chips – exemplified by the Eindhoven project – is the kind of strategy that makes sense in a globalised economy, says Joris Teer, policy analyst at the European Institute for Security Studies in Brussels.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: If the continent can take a lead in photonic chips, then future developments in AI and data will partly be dependent on Europe.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "Europe knows that its high energy and labour costs, skilled workforce shortages, and lack of private and public capital make an across-the-board reindustrialisation strategy impossible", Teer says.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "To retain influence, ensuring dependence on European parties rather than European autonomy is key." Once up and running, the Eindhoven project will provide a pilot production line which can be used multiple companies.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: It will be open to businesses across Europe and beyond, who can design and build chips without having to develop their own expensive production facilities.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: "What we want to establish here is what we call a foundry model; there's no intention to have our own product," Ton van Mol says.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Instead, they will produce to order for outside customers.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: It's the same idea which, at huge scale, has brought Taiwanese-based giant TSMC a position of global dominance in the manufacture of microchips.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Photonic chips are already in use, in highly specialised areas in data centres and in Lidar (light detection and ranging) sensor technology, for instance.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: For van Mol of TNO, helping the industry to scale up, by easing production challenges and increasing capacity, is the key step to moving them into the tech we use in our daily lives, like phones and laptops, and to drive innovation in areas like medical scanners and 6G communications.
sentences.article_title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave

sentences.text: Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

sentences.text: A jet engine will have hundreds of turbine blades Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: It is a true engineering marvel.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: "It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning." Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: "Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.
sentences.article_title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'

sentences.text: Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: UK and EU agree new deal for food exports, youth mobility and emissions but student fee talks to continue Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: At the dramatic conclusion of his first party conference speech as Labour leader in September - a moment he has been dreaming of for decades - the prime minister vowed to get closer to the EU.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Yet it does sound like there will be another summit next year - or, rather, an "informal brainstorming process" about potential options for future relations with the EU.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: That sounds pretty nebulous, sure, but an event dedicated specifically to both sides discussing how to change the terms of Britain's arrangements with the EU is likely to become quite a big moment when it arrives.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Perhaps as importantly, von der Leyen made clear that the EU was embracing this event too.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: That said, it does diminish the chances of major movement from Burnham towards embracing a specific model for the EU relationship in the intervening period.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: And what of the domestic politics of this?
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Britain's seventh prime minister in just over 10 years watched from Manchester as the fraught relationship with Europe wrecked the careers of so many of those predecessors.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Burnham's gamble is that this time it's different.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: He believes that public regret about how Brexit has played out opens the political space for a far-reaching renegotiation.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Plenty of Labour MPs enthusiastically agree, and see this as the route to uniting the "progressive" vote at the next election too.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Some, especially those who represent Labour's former industrial heartlands, are a little more apprehensive.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: This morning's confusion is a reminder that there is another element to this gamble.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Negotiating with Brussels, even if both sides believe progress is a "win-win", can be a fraught and complicated business.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: Once he's on the other side of his brainstorm, can Burnham carry that off without getting bogged down and distracting from his government's other priorities?
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: On the day he became Labour leader in July, Burnham described it as the biggest change moment in British politics in 40 years.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: He was talking principally about economic transformation.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: But going to Brussels and getting what he wants without serious complications would be a pretty big change too.
sentences.article_title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last

sentences.text: The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.
sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.article_title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

sentences.text: Yellow arrows indicate the tumours visible before treatment Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.text: Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.text: Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.text: But doctors stress it is unclear how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.

sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.text: The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting.
sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.text: "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.
sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.text: "We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue." Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.

sentences.text: Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.

sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.text: "We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

sentences.text: Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US .
sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.article_title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

sentences.article_title: Antibiotics saved my life - then nearly killed me

sentences.article_title: Antibiotics saved my life - then nearly killed me

sentences.text: "So, I had to go back to hospital then and have emergency antibiotics to basically stop me from getting sepsis." She had surgery and returned home but the pain persisted Davies believed the antibiotics made her ill.

sentences.article_title: Antibiotics saved my life - then nearly killed me

sentences.text: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Here's what you need to know.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Once established, it was effective.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible – and people have confidence in them.
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".
sentences.article_title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

sentences.text: It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.

sentences.text: Every month, more than 12,000 applications are made to Social Security Scotland for disability support.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The number of Scots receiving these benefits has risen sharply since the Covid pandemic, and is projected to hit one million by the end of the decade.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: This has been driven in part by younger people and claims for mental health conditions.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The cost of the system has been growing, posing additional challenges for Scottish ministers facing a tight budget settlement.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: But with the UK government considering a radical redesign of support in England and Wales, they insist that Scotland's welfare state does not need to be trimmed.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Why has there been such an increase in claims in Scotland, and can the government afford to continue its more generous approach?
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Scotland has long had a higher rate of ill health among adults than other parts of the UK, often attributed to its history of heavy industry and relatively high levels of poverty in certain areas.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: But the change seen in recent years has different roots.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: There has been a notable uptick in disability across the UK since the Covid pandemic - and it is most pronounced north of the border.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The percentage of Scotland's working-age population, aged 16 to 64, reporting having a disability increased from 19% in 2020-21 to 28% in 2023-24 , external .
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: In children aged under 16, it doubled from 6% to 12%.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: That has translated into a rising number of people receiving disability benefits - in total there are about 800,000 people in receipt of them today.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The Scottish Fiscal Commission says there has been a "shift in the age profile of applicants" since 2020.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Some 35% of the new applicants for Adult Disability Payment , external , since it was rolled out as Scotland's main disability benefit in 2022, have been people under 35.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Mental health is a key element in this, with 41% of the ADP caseload concerning "mental and behavioural disorders".
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Almost half of those are "neurotic and stress related" conditions, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: If you look back before social security was devolved to Holyrood, mental and behavioural disorders accounted for only 26% , external of the claims for Personal Independence Payments, the main disability payment in the UK system.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Among children, these conditions now account for 64% of applications in Scotland - with the number of people under 16 receiving the Child Disability Payment for them more than doubling from 30,000 in 2020 to 75,000 this year.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Meanwhile, mental health conditions play a much smaller role in benefit claims from older people, accounting for 13% of the Pension Age Disability Payment caseload - behind both back and joint issues and diseases of the circulatory system.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The pressure of social media and constant connectivity has been cited as a driver of mental distress There are inevitably some who characterise it as the product of an overly sensitive "snowflake generation".
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: But others note that the current cohort of young people spent their formative years in lockdown before emerging into a cost-of-living crisis and the destabilising rise of AI - with polling suggesting that the majority believe they will be worse off than their parents , external .
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Mental health charity Scottish Action for Mental Health (SAMH) says young people today are "growing up significantly more mentally distressed".
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Chief executive Billy Watson said they face a "relentless" pace of life, with social media constantly exposing them to unsettling news and world events and unrealistic social comparison.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Data published this week from the Scottish Health Survey , external suggested that mental wellbeing - measured using an internationally-recognised scoring system - had recovered to pre-pandemic levels.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: However, the 16 to 24 age group had the lowest score of any included, and around a quarter of young adults reported poor enough mental health to suggest a possible psychiatric disorder.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Young people have reported higher levels of anxiety and loneliness since lockdown An independent review for the UK government by Prof Peter Fonagy last month said the problems faced by young people were real , with dramatically increasing cases of mental distress including depression and anxiety.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: But Fonagy also warned of an "increasing risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis".
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: He said this was because "diagnosis has become the primary gateway to support that could and should be available earlier".
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: This was echoed by Alan Milburn, author of the UK government's review of support for young people in England and Wales.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: He said that "in too many places, diagnosis has inappropriately become the key that unlocks help", which has "created pressure on people to seek a diagnosis".
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: As an aside, it should be noted that while Milburn's review centred on employment prospects, benefit uptake does not always read across directly to this; Adult Disability Payment is not an "out of work" benefit like Jobseeker's Allowance.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The employment rate among disabled people in Scotland is more than 50%, and on the flip side studies have suggested , external that almost half of those not in education, employment or training are not claiming benefits either.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Alan Milburn's review could lead to a major shake-up of support in England and Wales Milburn's review , external proposed sweeping changes to the youth support network in England and Wales, including faster access to mental health services and a complete replacement of Personal Independence Payments.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: But in Scotland, "Pip" has already been replaced by Adult Disability Payment.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: There was a very deliberate wave of publicity around the launch of the new benefit in 2022 - alongside the versions for children and pensioners - in a bid to increase uptake among people who might have been entitled to the likes of Pip, but never claimed.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: With more money being spent on the Scottish system - it costs about £1bn a year over and above the block grant from Westminster - there is an easy narrative that it is inherently more generous.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: A report last year concluded that it was more " significantly more compassionate " and "kinder in tone and approach".
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: However, it is worth noting that more than half of initial applications for ADP have been rejected, with 43% approved compared with 54% denied - broadly in line with the system in England and Wales.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: There has been a steady increase in rejections since ADP was rolled out in 2022 - in the first few months only a quarter of applications were rejected, but over the past year it has been 67%.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Asked about this, Education Secretary Mairi McAllan said Social Security Scotland undertook a "very robust and close examination of all applications", and that people had to prove they were in need.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Last year also saw a record number of referrals rejected from NHS child mental health services , with ministers saying specialist services are only right for a small proportion of young people.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Mairi McAllan has said Scottish ministers will consider Milburn's report carefully Even with an increase in rejections, the overall number of claims and the cost of the devolved social security system has been rising - and ADP alone makes up more than half of the total cost.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The last forecast from the SFC was for the social security bill to be £7.8bn in 2027-28 - within that, ADP accounts for £4.2bn, the pension-age disability payment £972m and child disability payment £659m.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: By 2030-31, the cost is forecast to rise to £9.2bn - which has prompted questions from auditors and opposition parties alike about whether it is sustainable.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Ministers have repeatedly insisted that they view benefits as an investment in the people of Scotland.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: But they have also said they will look carefully at Milburn's proposals.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: A more generous system is not necessarily an easy choice, when it entails higher rates of income tax and cuts to other budgets.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: There is also the possibility that changes down south could widen the existing £1bn funding gap, by cutting welfare spending at Westminster.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: First Minister John Swinney has suggested that there are "potentially some significant financial implications that could be negative" for Holyrood.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: But if money cut from benefits ends up being spent on education or local employment services - devolved issues - it would end up flowing back into the Scottish budget regardless.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Milburn's plan could apparently save about £200m a year by 2036-37, and while this would grow in subsequent years it should not represent a huge impact on devolved budgets.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: And 10 years down the road the Scottish government's own public service reform plans, from the NHS to local councils, should have been worked through.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: Who knows where we will be by then?
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The pace of change is relentless - in technology, in society, and in the health of the nation.
sentences.article_title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

sentences.text: The question is whether governments and policy can keep up.

sentences.text: Midwife turnover in the Welsh NHS is at its lowest level for over 16 years Midwives who will graduate in Wales next year have been told there are fewer jobs available for them than expected.
sentences.article_title: Midwives told to expect fewer jobs as recruitment drive is paused

sentences.text: The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said this was in addition to the 66 newly qualified midwives who did not manage to find a job after they graduated last year .
sentences.article_title: Midwives told to expect fewer jobs as recruitment drive is paused

sentences.text: Director of RCM Cymru Julie Richards said the situation was "unacceptable" when maternity services were "facing pressure from every direction" .
sentences.article_title: Midwives told to expect fewer jobs as recruitment drive is paused

sentences.text: The Welsh government said it recognised the concerns around employment uncertainty and was working with NHS Wales "to understand workforce pressures and requirements".
sentences.article_title: Midwives told to expect fewer jobs as recruitment drive is paused

sentences.text: Kimmy Williams, 37, from Swansea has had to return to her old job working in the kitchen at a local college because there were not enough midwifery graduate jobs available in Wales.
sentences.article_title: Midwives told to expect fewer jobs as recruitment drive is paused

sentences.text: Williams said she was aware that almost half of her peers on the midwifery course at Swansea University were yet to find a job despite the promise of employment for everyone once they graduated.

sentences.text: "Now I'm just working in the same job I was previously but worse off financially," she added.
sentences.article_title: Midwives told to expect fewer jobs as recruitment drive is paused

sentences.article_title: What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?
